text_fidelity_a:
NexFoto 32GB Large 15 inch Digital Picture Frame, Wi-Fi Digital Photo Frame, Wall-Mountable, Instantly Share Photos Videos via App or Email, Gift for Father's Day This digital frame is a really nice size for displaying your photos. It can store a lot of them, and it has a decent brightness so you can easily see them even in a brightly lit room. The plastic frame isn't the nicest looking in my opinion; it would be nice if they offered different color and style frame options. I will probably end up painting my frame- I haven't quite figured how I plan to do that yet, but I just want it to look less like modern black plastic.

The app is really, truly terrible. It's difficult to figure out, it will only upload a few files at a time, and it takes forever, so if you have a lot of files to load, take my advice and don't even bother with the app. Just put them on a micro-SD card and load them that way.

Navigating the onboard menu is difficult, and I didn't find the directions to be very helpful. I was eventually able to get it figured out, more or less. There are some things that just don't make sense; for instance, in the main menu you can set the slide show to display the time each photo is shown. However, this doesn't actually do anything as far as I can tell, because after setting it the images will still flash by at 15 second intervals (this seems to be the default) until you go into the menu for the individual folder you are showing from and set the time intervals there. And the time options there are different than they are on the main menu; for instance, the main menu allows you to set 1 minute intervals. The folder menu allows 30 seconds and 2 minutes, but not 1 minute. So I'm not sure what all that's about.

Once you get it set up right, the picture looks very nice. It has an optional sleep mode you can set, and it has a motion sensor function you can enable if you like, but what I really wish it had was an ambient brightness sensor so that it would dim itself when the room is dark, and brighten itself when it gets brighter. This would be such a huge upgrade, especially for bedrooms, or TV rooms, or anywhere else where you want it to be dimmer when it's dark and brighter when it's bright.
text_fidelity_b: NexFoto 32GB Large 15 inch Digital Picture Frame, Wi-Fi Digital Photo Frame, Wall-Mountable, Instantly Share Photos Videos via App or Email, Gift for Father's Day

OontZ Angle 3 Bluetooth Speaker, Portable Wireless Bluetooth 5.0 Speaker, 10 Watts, Crystal Clear Stereo Sound, Rich Bass, IPX5 Water Resistant, Loud Portable Bluetooth Speaker (Black) I was very disappointed after reading so many positive reviews.

This unit was to be primarily used in my bathroom with my Iphone 6 while I get ready for work. It was to replace a JBL Charge I'd had for a few years and no longer would hold a charge.

The sound is strong, but tinny. No real depth or strong bass notes. I played several songs and really, really wanted it to work. Finally, I just gave up.

Now, the reason I gave it 2 stars is that it would be perfect for spoken-word use. It paired up fairly quick and the size is simply perfect for portability. And it is very attractive.

So I decided to give the Angle 3 Plus a shot for $7.00 more. Wow - what a difference! Sounds great, bass is perfect for the size, and I couldn't be happier.

Bottom line is that the choice is totally subjective on the part of the listener but, for the money, the Cambridge Angle 3 Plus is the way to go.

text_fidelity_a:
Soundcore by Anker Life P3i Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Earbuds, 4 Mics, AI-Enhanced Calls, 10mm Drivers, Powerful Sound, App for Custom EQ, 36H Playtime, Fast Charging, Transparency, Bluetooth 5.2 I’ve been using the Soundcore by Anker Life P3i Earbuds for about a month. For the price, they are a nice set of earbuds with some good features. The sound quality is above average. I’m not an audiophile; if I can clearly hear Billie Eilish songs, I’m happy.

On the downside, the ANC could be improved and the case itself doesn’t support wireless charging. The earbuds can be charged in the case, but the case itself charges via USB-C.

What I like:
🎧 The earbuds are comfortable. Of course, this is somewhat subjective. But I have a few inner ear piercings (rook, daith, and tragus) and some earbuds irritate my piercings. I can wear this pair for a few hours. And if needed, I can use one earbud at a time, you don’t have to use both for playback.

🎧 The controls are tactile, not touch. I personally dislike touch controls on earbuds, they’re way too easy to accidentally activate. To avoid pressing the earbuds deeper into my ears, I hold onto the “stem” part when using the buttons. The Soundcore app allows customization of the controls, you can change the settings for single tap, double tap, and hold.

What I don’t like:
🎧 The app requires an account to use. Just let me customize my settings without signing up.

🎧 The case can’t be charged wirelessly. It only has one LED status light on the outside. The light only turns red to indicate the case needs to be charged when it has 10% or less remaining.

🎧 The ANC is just okay. I can hear the TV about ten feet away from me.
text_fidelity_b: Soundcore by Anker Life P3i Hybrid Active Noise Cancelling Earbuds, 4 Mics, AI-Enhanced Calls, 10mm Drivers, Powerful Sound, App for Custom EQ, 36H Playtime, Fast Charging, Transparency, Bluetooth 5.2

text_fidelity_a:
Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker with aptX/AAC (Black) I’m a big fan of the Roar since it provides me with two key benefits: great sound and is easy to use. The Roar 2 retains those two benefits and adds one more: a smaller footprint. I’m going to try my best to not overuse the words “outstanding” and "impressive" in this review, but it’s going to be a challenge. This is an impressive speaker.

The out-of-the-box experience is nicely done. As expected at this price point, it comes in upscale packaging. More important, it comes with a pretty decent user guide. That’s significant since the Roar 2 has a lot of features – to call it just “a speaker” really shortchanges it. It’s also a recorder, a power bank, an MP3 player, an SD card reader, a speakerphone – it will even lull you to sleep with Bedtime Mode where it gradually decreases the volume and then powers off. My only complaint about the manual is that it’s physically small, which means the type size is also small. I do wish manufacturers would realize that those of us with aging eyes still like loud music!

And loud music is this product’s forte. I’m able to get room-filling sound while maintaining crisp highs, clear midrange and solid but not muddy bass. I can even go past room-filling to the “let’s annoy the neighbors” levels and still maintain impressive fidelity. Using the Tera Bass option boosts the bass response to the point where you would swear there was a separate subwoofer on the floor. You can see the end plates resonate to help drive the bass (plus it just looks really cool as well).

Day to day usage of the Roar 2 is straightforward even though there are so many features. All the buttons are labeled fairly clearly, albeit at times with small type. I would also have preferred a greater contrast to the labels since sometimes they are hard to see unless the Roar 2 is under a bright light. There are voice prompts for many key features which I found helpful. Normally I don’t care for voice prompts, but these were done in a natural sounding voice at a low volume making them not at all irritating. But, if you don’t like them at all, you can turn them off. There are small, but clear indicator lights to keep you apprised of battery charge level, settings, and other criteria.

The build quality is excellent. This feels as good as it looks, with a solid heft to it, an excellent quality metal grill, and quality plastic case components. All the buttons have a good tactile feel to them. I have it in white, which looks very nice with the gray contrast control pad. My only quibble is that some of the buttons/levers are on the small side. However, those tend to be the lesser used function. The main function buttons (on/off, volume, pairing, Tera Bass, etc.) are larger and easy to use.

The Roar 2 is not inexpensive, but the performance, build quality and features make it an excellent value. If you enjoy great sound and need to keep to a small footprint speaker, these should absolutely be on your short list (and at the top of it by a wide margin). Highly, highly recommend.
[Sample provided for review]
text_fidelity_b: Creative Sound Blaster Roar 2 Portable NFC Bluetooth Speaker with aptX/AAC (Black)

Garmin DriveSmart 51 NA LMT-S with Lifetime Maps/Traffic, Live Parking, Bluetooth,WiFi, Smart Notifications, Voice Activation, Driver Alerts, TripAdvisor, Foursquare (Renewed) This is my second order for the same refurbished unit.

The first one lasted 6 months before dying. However, I liked it, and I knew how to use it, so I ordered another one.

This one came without any charge so I charged it up for two days. That brought it up to 2/3 charge.

When I tried to set the options, the charge dropped to barely charged, and then the screen went dark.

I ordered a new unit this morning because it seems that refurbished units are nothing but junk.

Canon EF 100mm f/2.8L IS USM Macro Lens with UV Protection Lens Filter The Canon 100mm f/2.8 USM macro is a lovely lens already, and Canon would need to significantly improve on it to make any owner of this lens consider selling in order to upgrade to the new L version. The new Canon 100mm f/2.8 L USM macro lens with image stabilization fits the bill and this particular 100mm macro owner, at least, decided to upgrade. I rented this lens at first to try out the new features, as my older 100mm lens is one of my most-coveted, most-used lenses, and I didn't want to give up on it simply because there was a new kid on the block. After the instant rebates came around I was in a well-enough informed position to make the purchase, and at a good price.

The aforementioned Image Stabilization is very effective in situations where you can't use the tripod, but want to maintain critical focus while working with shallow depth of field. The IS system in this lens, to boot, is an improvement on Canon's IS system found in other earlier lenses - Hybrid IS, a system which is particularly tuned to the demands of macro photography; I've tested this with the new lens and it's amazing what I can successfully capture handheld that previously absolutely necessitated a tripod. You can get the same results handheld now with approximately 3-4 less stops of light than you could previously. This perfectly suits my shooting style - I like to roam around, usually sans tripod, and take images in natural surroundings that may not always have the best available light. A relatively slow shutter speed to capture the scene in front of me usually meant I'd have to compensate by ratcheting up the ISO or go wider with the aperture, which are not always or often good compromises, for image quality reasons as well as for reasons of creative choice. The IS is a much welcome feature, and provides more leeway in variable lighting. Also sometimes people complain that the IS is too noisy when in operation; while that can certainly be true (I have a couple of other Canon lenses with IS), I have found that the new IS system in this latest lens is noticeably quieter - I'd call it pretty quiet, even with nothing else to compare it to.

Out of focus highlights - the bokeh - is smooth, smoother than the older version. Images appear very crisp, I'm pleased with the sharpness. The new lens is about an ounce or so heavier than the older one, not so much that you'd really notice. Also the lens, while a L, does not have the same build appearance as other L lenses - it is not hefty and metallic, and cream-colored. That doesn't bother me so much, but others more invested in the distinctive look of Canon L lenses might care. The lens body itself is sleek (compared to the rather portly older model) and has a nice matte black finish which you can handle easily - I don't quite know how to describe it - it doesn't have the usual "slippery" metal feel to it, so you don't feel like you might drop it if you aren't careful. Because it's an L, it comes with a lens hood; I always get hoods for my lenses, so I love it when a lens has one included!

One thing that is an interesting feature is that there are three settings for the Autofocus limiter (the older lens has two). It's basically there to help speed the AF in finding its optimal focus depending on which camera-to-subject distance you are shooting with - anywhere from strictly close up (.3 to .5 meter of distance) to full range. I'm still trying to figure out what real time difference it makes to choose between the .3m-to-infinity limiter and .5m-to-infinity limiter, but I assume it must make some difference for Canon to have included the additional option. Early days yet, I'll figure it out.

All in all - not every lens redesign results in a lens worth ditching an old model for, especially when the upgrade entails a bit more cost. But the new 100mm macro L is very much worth the upgrade, and the IS is a welcome addition to Canon's most popular macro option. Now if they'll just put IS in the 180mm...

I will also add that I made this particular purchase through the Marketplace seller J&R. I had no problems with them - delivery was swift and the item was well-packed.
text_fidelity_b: Canon EF 100mm f/2.8L IS USM Macro Lens with UV Protection Lens Filter

Pixel Mago Canon Speedlite ETTL High Speed 5D2 5D3 6D 7D 60D External Speedlite While this flash doesn’t outperform the Canon Speedlite, it comes the closest of any of the Speedlite “clones” I’ve tried so far, and does so with impressive build quality.

I was impressed with this right out of the box mainly due to the care taken with packaging. No, packaging doesn’t impact the performance of the flash, but it does take the worry out of getting one that is damaged due to UPS handling. The flash is packed in a carry case (which is very well-made and has cushioning) and, in turn, packed inside of an air-filled tube case. Together they provide more than ample protection against transit-born bruises short of being run over by the UPS truck.

The flash feels very solid. The head articulates up/down/left/right and has indents at the most commonly used angles. The head is a bit stiff to move, but I consider that as a positive since I don’t want the head getting bumped out of place when I have it positioned the way I want it.

The hotshoe frame is plastic but feels very solid. There’s a rotating locking ring to keep it in place while on the camera. It made contact and worked just fine on a 5D Mark II, a 4D and a Rebel.

The battery compartment door has a spring-loaded hinge so it pops up when unlatched. Again, good build quality on that (which is a common point of failure on other low-cost flashes I’ve used). It uses 4 AA batteries. It ran fine on rechargeables.

The control panel and LCD screen are both easy to use and see for the most part. The buttons beep when pressed, but that can be turned off if you want a silent operation. Some of the icons on the screen are very small – I needed to squint a bit to make some of them out. Then again, my aging eyes could be a contributing factor.

Most of the commands are executed by pressing a button and then selecting options using a rotating wheel. The wheel is the only part that didn’t work all that well at times. Sometimes a single twist moved it through the menu; other times I needed to twist it a couple of times to get it to register.

The capabilities of this flash are very impressive given the price point. It offers synch flash, manual flash, curtain synch, up to 1/8000 second synch, master/slave mode, AF assist beam, TTL flash, zoom settings and an LED lamp. It also has a nice amount of convenience features such as auto off (with various timed settings ranging from 5 minutes to 2 hours), a lock mode, screen on/off and test mode. It even has a USB port that can be used to update the firmware should updates be available (at this writing I am not aware of any updates).

The manual is not great. It offers a decent listing of the capabilities, but is often sparse in pointing out the details. But, if you have some measure of experience with a flash, it’s not hard to figure out (with a bit of experimenting) how to use it.

Given the price, this is an excellent value. It probably won’t suit the needs of a professional photographer but for an amateur (even a very avid one) it’s an excellent alternative to Canon gear at a much nicer price.
text_fidelity_b: Pixel Mago Canon Speedlite ETTL High Speed 5D2 5D3 6D 7D 60D External Speedlite

text_fidelity_a:
REOLINK 4K Security Camera Outdoor System, Surveillance IP PoE Camera with Human/Vehicle/Pet Detection, 25FPS Daytime, 100F IR Night Vision, Work with Smart Home, Up to 256GB SD Card, RLC-810A Fantastic camera. One of those items that screamed quality right out of the box. Good build, compact size, and has a waterproof connector for your Ethernet cable. Can be mounted where the cable comes through a hole in a fascia board behind the camera or where the cable comes out the side of the base. Base is infinitely adjustable. Camera has slight overhang on the top to keep water off the lens. Three pigtail cables - RJ-45 female connector can be the single cable if you have PoE or you can power this via a 12v power adapter or cable (local or centralized) for versatility.

This is my first IP camera, but I've used many analog cameras and DVRs.

I've hooked this up three ways: By itself, to a switch on the same network as a stand-alone NVR, and to a switch on the same network utilizing my QNAP NAS as the NVR - in each case powered by PoE. Here are some details I've figured out in the process:

---By itself: You can view it quickly and easily without delay with the App, which seems to have all the things you'd expect from a camera viewing app. I assume you can record to or snapshot to an SD card from the description, but I'm going to record to my network, so I didn't try that feature. This was just plug and play, worked super easy.

What I love is that once you figure out the IP address, you can access the camera via a webserver, which pretty much future-proofs the hardware. I despise "smart" devices where you need an app, because then you're at their mercy to run their app on whatever OS they decide to use and they can force you to make accounts, update, etc. Having this open to the user/owner is the way to go. Bravo.

And that web server is full featured. I was able to play around and do everything here before I bothered downloading the app.

Note that - like every camera I've ever used - the viewing software sends a substream which is lower resolution unless you demand the higher resolution. With the app you can see low and medium resolution, but 4k has trouble playing over WiFi (or else it's just smart enough to realize my screen can't support it anyway). Just pointing this out so you realize if you're seeing pixels, that doesn't mean the camera isn't actually recording at 4k.

---With NVR: I recently acquired a cheap 8-channel 4k NVR that I believe to be a Uniview OEM. I added a hard drive and put it on the same network as this camera. The NVR has an 8 port PoE switch built in, but it must also be a router, because it wants to use a different subnet if you put the camera on the NVR's switch. Otherwise, you can easily point the NVR to the camera via IP address.

So...if you point the NVR to the camera via IP address, you can view the camera from its own app or from the NVR app. I assume this still takes one of the NVRs 8 channels. This might be useful if you want to give someone access to just one camera on your network. But it occurred to me that, setup this way, you have constant data streaming over your network, and after you add quite a few cameras in 4k, this is going to start adding up.

If you put the camera directly on the NVR, you'll have to change the IP manually to match the subnet, or maybe you'll somehow get it to work through the NVR or with DHCP. I hadn't bothered spending time figuring this out yet because at the time I thought I'd just use my other switch, but I'm thinking once I get more cameras, it'll probably make more sense to put them directly onto the NVR and ...actually, then I won't have to change my entire IP scheme since I won't have so many new devices to organize.

I'm certain I can get it all working in unison with no problem, but it is more complicated than if you just buy an NVR set with a bunch of cameras already ready to work together. Either way shouldn't be a problem if you have IP knowledge, but I'm guessing a random homeowner might prefer a set.

---Using my NAS as NVR. Hmmm...a little disappointed with QNAP in this regard. I mean, I have three NASs, and I'm assuming they all have 2 licenses included, but to combine them into one program then I believe requires yet another license. I'm not into licenses, even if they're a one time deal, because that means you need accounts and if something happens where they're lost, you can run into all kinds of other issues. I just think consumers need to stand up to this sort of thing. But anyway, I had two included, so I tried it out:

I realized that this is a lot of work for my little consumer grade NAS, and even if I had a more hardcore NAS, I'm not sure I want resources being used all the time. It seems like I couldn't get it to use H.265 compression, nor could I get it to record at the higher resolutions and frame rates. Again, I didn't play with this too awful much once I got it recording and working because I already realized I definitely like the stand alone DVR better. The QNAP even had extra stuff to download and windows to pop up on your PC and all this other stuff. Just not as streamlined as I had hoped.

----Conclusion is that the camera is awesome. I'm not sure many are any better at this point. If you want something that just works easy and you don't know much about networking, you may wish to just buy an NVR set. But if you are IP capable, I think buying components separately could be a great way to go because you can really customize what you want to do. But as always, more options with networking means more potential headaches. But I am pretty certain that once you get it working the way you want it, you should be able to forget all about it and have it work indefinitely.

Oh, and after all that, I shouldn't forget to point out that I'd be thrilled to have this all by itself watching my porch just so I can tell when there's a package out there. My Ring (that came with the house) can't even see that because of the angle it is set at.
text_fidelity_b: REOLINK 4K Security Camera Outdoor System, Surveillance IP PoE Camera with Human/Vehicle/Pet Detection, 25FPS Daytime, 100F IR Night Vision, Work with Smart Home, Up to 256GB SD Card, RLC-810A

text_fidelity_a:
Click 'n Dig Model E4 Key Finder. 4 Receivers. Wireless RF Remote Item, Wallet Locator Okay, this is an update to the one-star review I emitted originally. The Click 'n' Dig folks are definitely getting their money's worth from their PR people, whom I would hire myself if I could afford to hire someone who works that hard. After viewing my crabby review (below), they got in touch and offered to send a new set (you get the key finder and several other pieces that you can attach to other easily lost items). Surely, said they, the set shipped to me must have been defective. Would I take another one and if it improved, would I consider re-reviewing?

Oh, why not? I have nothing else to do during the hours left around the seven 14-hour days a week entailed in running a business. :-D They sent the doodads in the mail.

MEANWHILE... Between the time I first posted my original grutch and the time the new package of goodies arrived, I lost my keys not once, not twice, but THREE TIMES.

Each time, the Key Finder located the things! Inside a purse...on a piece of furniture where I'd dropped the keys to rescue the dog...atop a countertop where no one in their right mind would ever leave their keys...

It's not a matter of standing wherever you happen to be and clicking the "finder" device. You do have to walk around the house, and you do have to point the finder in several directions until it locates and connects with the receiver on your keyring. Its signal will pass through some but not all walls (why, I do not know: possibly electrical wiring or insulation?). Its range is about 20 feet, I'd guess. It requires some patience and persistence on your part, but it does eventually work.

Click 'n' Dig sent me a new set, which I gave to some dear friends who are even more superannuated than I after the Missus expressed dismay at having lost her keys once again. This is one of those tools that makes old age tolerable...maybe even survivable.

***********

ORIGINAL WHINGE: Not sending this back, because I don't have time to hassle with repackaging and mailing. But can't recommend it. These devices are supposed to emit a 90-decibel beep when you point the hand-held radio transmitter at them. Thus if you have one on, say, a key ring, you should be able to locate the keys if you misplace them around the house. We're told the radio frequency goes through walls and has an 80-foot range.

Well, if that's 90 decibels, then 90 decibels isn't very loud. According to Purdue University, 90 db is as loud as a "Boeing 737 or DC-9 aircraft at one nautical mile (6080 ft) before landing (97 dB); power mower (96 dB); motorcycle at 25 ft (90 dB). Newspaper press (97 dB)." Dang! I wish!! If aircraft made the same level of sound as this handy-dandy beeper, the skies would be a lot quieter around here!! :-D And my neighbor's Harley would be a lot more fun, too...

No, the signal does not go through walls.

The range is about 25 feet. Any further away than that, and the transmitter will not elicit a beep. If your keys have dropped out of your pocket and slipped under a chair cushion, you have to be right on top of the chair to get receiver to beep.

Could be the gadgets need new batteries, which are kindly included. But the instructions do not show how to find the battery cases or how to open them. On the key fob, it's obvious enough where the battery case is, but you can't get it open -- I split a fingernail and hurt my finger when I tried. On the flat gadgets that you can stick to objects with the provided double-sided tape, I can't even find a CLUE to where a battery case could be opened. ?????????

The idea behind this device is truly brilliant. Sure do wish the execution were better.
text_fidelity_b: Click 'n Dig Model E4 Key Finder. 4 Receivers. Wireless RF Remote Item, Wallet Locator

text_fidelity_a:
bmanl Wireless Earbuds Bluetooth Headphones 48hrs Play Back Sport Earphones with LED Display Over-Ear Buds with Earhooks Built-in Mic Headset for Workout Purple BMANI-VEAT00L I purchased these to replace the Mpow Flame light that I had lost one of the earbuds too. I have gone through a couple of these.

What I do like is the charging case. It is pretty slim, it is USB C, and it also has a display to show how much of a charge it has. This is super helpful. It also has volume and connect/disconnect buttons. This has not yet had any charging issues, but I have not owned it for very long.

Now for what I don't like- They do not fit my ear that well. It may be the shape of hook, the length of the arm from which the speaker is mounted, or some other variable. The hook keeps it in place, but it never feels as if it's in my ear properly. I also think the sound is not so hot, and for 50 dollars I was expecting more. It is a little treble heavy on the heavier frequencies and just sounds like a cheap driver.

My previous headphone was the MPow Flame Lite. The charging case is bulkier and bare and there is no digital display. With that said- these are now 1/3 of the price. What I do like is that they fit my ear like a glove, and the sound quality is phenominal. It sounds like a much bigger driver. I am not an audiophile, but it really sounds great. Maybe it is the mid that come in fuller giving it a rich sound.

I have had some charging issues. Sometimes I find that only one of the headphones are dead and the other is fully charged. However, fit and sound are my most important details so these are my favorite. For the price I can purchase three and keep them in different places. If I lose one or have a charging issue I can replace it with the extra. This makes much more sense than keeping the aI do not more.

Edit: I changed from 3 to 5 stars. I have owned these now for almost one year, and use them probably every day. There has been no decrease in performance or battery life. I was so accustomed to my previous ear buds that I did not like these much at first. However, the sound is balanced, the battery life is great, and I really like the charging case. I have never actually times the batter life, but it is probably about 7-8 hours on a full charge. There are sooo many choices now for bluetooth ear buds, but these are a safe bet and most people should be happy. I am however not an audiophile, and someone who truly is may want to spend more on a Bose, or whatever the best ear buds are nowadays. My previous ones were more bass heavy, but these are better balanced. They do stay in the ear, unless I go to lay down on my back; I then have to push them back into my ear.
text_fidelity_b: bmanl Wireless Earbuds Bluetooth Headphones 48hrs Play Back Sport Earphones with LED Display Over-Ear Buds with Earhooks Built-in Mic Headset for Workout Purple BMANI-VEAT00L

Hiearcool Docking Station,11IN1 USB C Docking Station,Dual Monitor Laptop Docking Station USB C Dock for Dell HP Lenovo Universal Docking Station for Office and Work from Home This device it NOT worth it. I encourage everyone to buy a legitimate docking station. This device is designed to be a space-saver, but it cannot handle the demands.

I had this product suggested to me by a friend who was using it for two screens with our work laptop and it seemed to be working fine. I only used it for one screen in the beginning and the very first thing I noticed with it was that it would become very warm or hot to the touch after less than an hour. I used it for a few months and the next thing it did was cause my mouse and screens to lag behind during operation. I then purchased a camera that I tried to plug into this docking station and everything went even more haywire with the camera, mouse and screens both acting up when operating my laptop, and of course the device was always warm to hot. So, I stopped using it and just direct wired everything to my laptop, which is extremely inconvenient when I need to move my laptop around, and I don't have enough ports to plug things in. Then, my husband bought a new CPU and needed to plug his two screens in so I let him try this docking station, and it wouldn't even register with the CPU at all. I plugged it back into my laptop where I knew it did work at one time, and sure enough, it doesn't work anymore.

So, basically it didn't function the way it should have, and within 6 months it just stopped working all together. Biggest waste of money, and now I can't return it.
text_fidelity_b: Hiearcool Docking Station,11IN1 USB C Docking Station,Dual Monitor Laptop Docking Station USB C Dock for Dell HP Lenovo Universal Docking Station for Office and Work from Home

text_fidelity_a:
Philips ShoqBox SB7200 Bluetooth Wireless Speaker (Black) This is a great little speaker, a wonderful addition to your Bluetooth enabled smartphone.

Hooking up is easy. You simply press the button to turn on. You then turn on the bluetooth settings on your phone and put it in search mode. Within seconds your phone finds the device and pairs with it. Identifying it as a bluetooth headset. You can then play music directly from your phone through the speaker. I use google music, so I streamed my music, and then played it right to the Shoqbox.

Volume is controlled by a sliver knob on the top of the speaker. The speaker can be played laying down, or standing upright. It has great sound, with deep rich bass and clear mid and high ranged. It plays music well, but it shines with voice. I listen to podcasts and audio books alot and a spoken voice sounds superb on this.

Since my car does not have a port to pay my phone with, I take this in the car and use it to listen to podcasts and audio books with in the car. The volume level is high and clear enough to hear well in the car.

The unit is charged with the included micro USB cable. If you have a modern phone or electronic device (save for the iPod/iPad) you probably already have a micro USB charger, and this will also work with those, and add an additional charger to your collection. It also has a USB charger for connecting to your computer. Be warned, since this uses a bit of power to charge, it has a double USB Charger, so you'll need two available USB ports to charge your speaker.

It also has audio warning that tells you if your batter is full in a pleasing female voice (plenty of battery) or getting empty (half way on battery), or battery empty.

The only drawback is that I could not get the motion controlled audio controls to work that well, I had a bit of an issue with pausing and skipping forward. Also, if the battery gets below about 25%, audio quality is diminished, especially if you are using this as a speaker for a phone call.

Overall a great unit, with wonderful sound, easy setup and ease of use.
text_fidelity_b: Philips ShoqBox SB7200 Bluetooth Wireless Speaker (Black)

text_fidelity_a: Fitbit Flex Wireless Activity + Sleep Wristband, Slate, Small/Large If you hate the thought of wasting money on something that will just end up falling off your wrist, then DO NOT BUY THIS PRODUCT. I purchased two Fitbit Flex models, one for myself and one for my husband, on April 30, 2015. I didn't buy them from Amazon, but I did buy them from an authorized retailer. By October, my husband had quit wearing his because it wouldn't sync (we figured out this was easily fixed by restarting the phone the Fitbit app was installed on). He put his up and I continued wearing mine. During this time, my Fitbit started unlatching and falling off my wrist occasionally. I would find it laying around, or would notice, then retrace my steps and find the tracker. Fast forward to January: my Fitbit tracker fell off and was lost for good. I couldn't find it anywhere. I assume some lucky soul found it and calls it their own now. I started wearing my husband's tracker at this time with no issues. Then in March, it fell off my wrist in the parking lot of my office. I didn't notice this until it was too late. Someone I work with found it and returned it to me. Unfortunately, it was ran over by a vehicle (judging by the marks on the band) and crushed. No more Fitbit. Full disclosure: I tended to play with the fastener on my first Fitbit, though I made myself not do that anymore after losing it and using the second one. I also had 9 total bands with which I used the Fitbits in  this review. I though rotating between the bands daily would keep the fastenings tighter and reduce the risk of losing my Fitbit. Not so. When I decided to contact Fitbit and ask if they might be able to help me remain a loyal customer by giving me a percentage off my next Fitbit purchase, they obliged after a string of emails back and forth, sending me an email code to be used ONLY on their website. The discount was for 25% off, which is the everyday price on many of their items on Amazon. I should have pushed for more, but I didn't realize that until I went to compare their web prices with those on Amazon. In short, I feel like I dropped $200+ on Fitbit products and all of that money was lost. Their products with a watchband type fastener seem to be better, so my only caveat is that if you choose to buy the Flex, be prepared to lose it. I am currently without a tracker and have thought about buying one, but I am gun shy when it comes to dropping another $150 on a Fitbit Charge HR (has a watchband fastener) when I know the company doesn't stand behind their products. Sorry, Fitbit.
text_fidelity_b: Fitbit Flex Wireless Activity + Sleep Wristband, Slate, Small/Large

text_fidelity_a:
Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red) [[VIDEOID:c23012732deceb9d78b96d41ac89bfcb]] [[VIDEOID:56e6589f81a80deb1709b51fc87a42ef]] [[VIDEOID:bdf9b77251e219b84bed6372225dbf2a]] [[VIDEOID:838bfc2c03ad2a6d884b05f4a37eddbe]] [[VIDEOID:f7f3bb80516774e2cc828f076249211a]] [[VIDEOID:d48cd1a96b9a119e675001d320845a53]] [[VIDEOID:9363c8a20797fe64545aeb51179ca502]] [[VIDEOID:3371609d21e77efbab0cfd0f6265a782]] This is a terrific little action camera that has remarkable clear video, good audio and is extremely easy to use. I understand there were some problems with audio in the earlier versions, but it seems to be all fixed now because the sound quality was excellent when tested both indoors and outside.

I won't bore you with going over all of the specs which you can read in the product description, but I'll tell you how easy it is to use. Mine arrived partially charged, so I used my fingernail to open the back port and inset the included 8gb micro SD card, then charged it fully within an hour. On a full battery it can operate for about 107 minutes and when depleted it takes between 1.5 to 2 hrs to fully charge.

I downloaded the app to my iPad for free from the app store, then did some testing. It connected easily to my WiFi and the interface understandable and easy to use giving you the choice to shoot still photos or videos in several different resolutions. You can also import the photos or videos taken with the camera to your cell phone, your iPad, or share them using the WiFi connection to import them.

This little camera takes gorgeous high def photos, and the audio inside is crystal clear. When I was offered the opportunity by the manufacturer to test the Cube+ I went ahead and purchased a [[ASIN:B00NXK3JTI Polaroid Helmet Mount for the Polaroid CUBE, CUBE+ HD Action Lifestyle Camera]] so I would be able to properly test it in action in order to determine video and sound quality outside in the elements.

I attached the helmet mount to my 9 y/o granddaughter's helmet, placed the Cube+ in it, started it through the app on my iPad and sent her out on her scooter to see how the video and audio quality was. I've attached a short part of the video here so you can assess it for yourself, but I'm quite pleased with the quality of both the picture and the sound, and I didn't experience any lag time in regards to the app.

It does record video in MP4 format, so if you have trouble hearing the audio on your computer you should download QuickTime Player or VLC Player. Both downloads are free and should allow you to view the files and hear the audio. VLC also has a free converter available in case you prefer to use Windows Media Player or Windows Movie Maker. I use a free app called Trim & Cut on my iPad which shortens, condenses, and converts my videos to the format I prefer, and that's what I used for the video I've attached here.

This is a reasonably priced tough little action camera that's easy to use and produces great quality video. It's weather resistant and splashproof so it can handle the outdoors already, but I plan to buy the waterproof case for it so we can have fun swimming with it on this summer. I don't own a GoPro, so I have nothing to compare this to, but from a user's stand point I can definitely tell you that this is user friendly, easy to operate and does a remarkably good job! Enjoy!

This camera was provided at no cost by the manufacturer for evaluation and review.
text_fidelity_b: Polaroid Cube+ 1440p Mini Lifestyle Action Camera with Wi-Fi & Image Stabilization (Red)

With free super saver shipping, it arrived in about a week and a half and it was exactly as I expected it would be from reading the reviews. It is true what several of the reviews have mentioned, the screws that come with it truly do not hold the end cap in the case (which means that the hard drive can slip in and out). Another thing that's been mentioned is that there is no way to turn the enclosure off, i.e. if the drive is plugged into the computer it will be on regardless of if the computer is on or not (at least in my experience).

Audio-Technica ATH-LS50iSBK In-Ear Monitor Headphones with In-Line Mic & Control, Black Very good headphones. Rubber ear tips are comfortable for long periods of time and 3 different sizes of replacement tips are included. Bass is very good and overall sound clarity is much better than with cheap headphones. Full volume is more than loud enough for me and distortion at the highest volume is tolerable (unlike with cheap headphones). Wrap-around cables can be a hassle, but these have thicker wires and don't tangle as much as others that I have tried. Wrap-around cables really prevent the earbuds from falling out when I am working out. A simple nylon bag is the only carrying case included in the oversized box, but better cases are available at dollar stores.

Yes, Apple is trying to kill off wired headphones, but wired headphones still have huge advantages over Bluetooth, such as not having to worry about battery life, being able to recharge your phone at the same time you are listening to music, and of course the sound quality of wired headphones is usually better than similarly priced Bluetooth headphones.

text_fidelity_a:
Etymotic Research MC5 Noise-Isolating In-Ear Earphones I bought these to supplement my ER6i phones which I enjoy and have had no problems with. Unfortunately, they are no longer made so I bought these which I felt would be equivalent. That turned out to not be the case. The sound isolation is lacking, no matter how far they are jammed into my ear canals - it seems they may be purposely letting in some med/high end frequencies to give the phones a more open sound. In my case it seems to heighten certain ambient noises I am interested in blocking - running fans especially. Microphony from the dangling cables seems to be more noticeable too.

These guys have to absolutely invade my ear canals whereas the ER6i phones would need to just barely enter my ear to make a seal. The result is very noticeable and eventually uncomfortable.

The wires are thicker which seems nice at first, but they just get in the way - the thinner wires of the ER6i would pretty much fall into place and not be a nuisance.

All in all, I could tell these were unacceptable within a half hour of use and they are going back.

text_fidelity_a:
Samsung UN55NU8000FXZA Flat 55" 4K UHD 8 Series Smart LED TV (2018) If you’re someone who obsesses over every minute picture detail, this may not be the TV for you. But, if you just want to watch a great picture and not have the purchase break the bank, this should absolutely be on your short list.

I looked at quite a few TVs and read a LOT of tech reviews. But, while the OLEDs and QLEDs did look better than this when side-by-side, in my living room this is providing an excellent picture, both for 4K as well as older SD and HD content. I’m 100% satisfied with the picture quality, both when watched in a bright room and in the dark. 4K content is especially “wow” inspiring!

Setup, including Internet access and tuning the picture quality, was straightforward.

The overall design is very nice, with a very minimal frame. The stand is attractive, although I did end up wall mounting it after having it for a short while.

The smart features are nice, but I don’t use them much since I stream using a Fire box. But, it’s nice having easy access to sources that are not readily reachable via the Fire box, such as YouTube and Google Playstore. The user interface for the smart features is pretty initiative.

I also can’t speak to how good the speakers are since I’m running this through an AV receiver, and not using the TVs speakers.

Complaints are minor. I’m not a fan of the remote since I prefer a more “button dense” design than the minimal design Samsung uses. I also don’t care for the rubberized coating they have on the remote. Other minor complaints are that there’s no easily accessible on/off button on the TV itself (it’s hidden behind the red remote sensor at the base), and that the voice command system is not very polished or effective as of yet.

At the current price (plus the 15% discount from Chase) this is an outstanding value for a 65 inch TV that has a lot of features, decent build quality, excellent performance, and an attractive design.
text_fidelity_b: Samsung UN55NU8000FXZA Flat 55" 4K UHD 8 Series Smart LED TV (2018)

My home internet is horribly slow so for me, it’s speedier to put the files on a flash drive.

ETUCRAY Headphone Jack Adapter for Phone Dongle Aux Audio to 3.5mm Cables Earphone Adaptor Headset Splitter for Music&Charger This timer is a good size with a very readable LED display and a strong magnet on the clip on the back to hold it to your fridge or whatever a magnet will stick to. The buttons are large and accessible, and it's really no problem to set it up. It beeps loudly when the time is up, so there's little danger you're not going to hear it from an adjoining room.

Strangely, on day one (unlike with some timers I've used), the first three or four times that I held down the hour, minute, or second buttons to speed up the counting and turn off the beeps, it just froze and stopped counting. If I pressed the button over and over to advance the counter by one, it worked—beeping annoyingly loudly each time, of course. I was about to give it a two-star review and throw it away because I couldn't stand it, but I put off doing it and just stuck it to the top of my stove. A week later, after I'd used the stove several times and the timer probably got exposed to some heat, I went back to try it again so I could write this review and the fast-count sans beeps feature worked. Weird. Maybe it was just stressed in shipping and needed time to settle down....

A few things I really do dislike is that it's easy to reset the time by mistake if the grey button on the left gets slid up; the modes are manually set with this button. (That approach to the modes could be good for the technologically challenged, though.) Also, if you overshoot your mark on the time, there is no way to go backward; you have to go forward until you come back around to where you were supposed to have stopped the first time. The clip is a little too sharply angled, so when you stick the timer to a surface with the magnet, the face slants down somewhat, but it's still visible; really not that big of a deal.

Another thing, as I've remarked about another MeasuPro product: the how-to info on the packaging is white letters on light grey, which is practically unreadable for anyone, not just people like me with old eyes. (The company told me they were correcting that with the other product, so I expect they will do the same with this one.)

text_fidelity_a:
HP ENVY Desktop Computer, Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB Hard Drive & 512 GB SSD Storage, Windows 10 Pro (TE01-1254, 2020 Model) It is an alright system if you are only going to be doing basic computing like Microsoft Office, email, and some Netflix (but maybe not all at the same time). However, at a current price of over $850 being saddle with only the onboard graphics is hardly acceptable. Second, this system is also only okay if you never plan to repair the computer if there are issues with the power supply or motherboard. If you toss out your systems when they break, then this will work. If you like to swap out the bad parts, run for the hills you do not want to be stuck dealing with the HP part store.

If you want to play any games or use programs that require a bit more heavy lifting, (design software, CAD, or anything pulling a bunch of images or rendering) or need to have several programs running at once, you are going to struggle without a graphics card.

But can't you just add your own Graphics Card, I mean it is 2020 after all? Well... while this system does have an open slot on the motherboard for the addition of a graphics card it is severely handicapped in using it. For one, it is a very small case and you will be stuck with a small form factor card, which tend to be more expensive than their standard size counterparts. Worse yet, the included system power is only 180 watts. You cannot run much past whatever is already in the system with that, so you will need to also upgrade the power supply. Here is where it gets annoying. HP not only uses their own motherboard (Baker in this system) but the motherboard uses a proprietary connection to the power supply, so you HAVE TO BUY their power supply and only theirs. There is not an adapter, I looked and looked and looked some more.

That means heading over to the HP parts store website and trying not to pound your head into a wall with how backwards and outdated their system is. If you manage to locate the ONLY 400 watt power supply that works with the baker motherboard (yes 400 watt is the biggest they make that work for this case and motherboard) you will be hit with a $125 price tag (more like $150 after tax and shipping) for a power supply that should really cost half that. Which even if it says is in stock, will likely be back-ordered. They told me I'd be lucky to see it in 2 months even if it says "instock" in the system. Because they are the only ones selling it, you have to either wait or just forget about the upgrade. If you NEED it because your current power supply isn't working, well too bad for you.

If you have hung in this far and managed to get the power supply squared away, you can start on the graphics card piece. Now here is where it gets fun, you will want to avoid the HP parts store. They have the GTX 1660ti listed but its price bounces from over $1000 (yes a grand) to around $700 for a card that is about $300 on Amazon. Due to the power supply limitations a 1660ti is as high as you are going to be able to get, which puts you on par with an entry level gaming laptop. Due to size limitations of the HP Envy case you will want to stick to a small form factor card (generally that means one fan not two, but measure first some of those single fans are still a bit long).

So between the $150 power supply (that you may never get) and the ($300 graphics card off amazon) you are looking at about $450 in an upgrade to basically keep pace with a low level gaming laptop that costs less than what you paid for the HP Envy to begin with.

Which is my biggest problem with this system and the reason for the 3 stars, because it only does what it says (so earns its 3 stars) BUT if it has any sort of hardware issue down the line or doesn't meet your needs, you are going to be stuck buying a whole new system or be left to the mercy of HPs terribly unreliable part store with its over inflated prices and unreliable delivery timetables.
text_fidelity_b: HP ENVY Desktop Computer, Intel Core i7-10700, 16 GB RAM, 1 TB Hard Drive & 512 GB SSD Storage, Windows 10 Pro (TE01-1254, 2020 Model)

I hadn't necessarily heard of Gosky before, but I gather they are a big brand in optics. I'm also going on relatively little education on the subject that a monocular is easier to focus at longer distances and/or a larger range of distances because you don't have to focus the two lenses - something which makes it hard for me to look through binoculars after a while.

This is pretty lightweight, but feels very solid and nice. It has a turn-out piece to the rear of the rear lens to accommodate people who don't wear glasses. And besides that, there is only one knob to turn to focus, mostly depending on the distance to the object of your attention.

The carry case is fairly rugged nylon and has a belt loop, but not the kind of belt loop you can use without unstrapping your belt. It's also a little large for a belt in my opinion, but may come in handy. The hand strap is pretty nice, but there is a lot of extra length to the strap I really don't know what to do with, and I feel like the actual attachment process could be more refined. I do really like that both lens covers can stay attached to the body while not in use (rear one can be attached to the hand strap and front on is attached to a rubber ring which stays on the body) which makes for a refined and complete product.

Not sure if this one can accommodate a cell phone holder or not...seems like people must take pictures through these things when birding or spying or watching opera or whatever they're doing.

Nice product. I now have a good feeling about this brand that was previously off my radar.

text_fidelity_a:
Everstone Adjustable Tilt TV Wall Mount Bracket for Most 32-90 Inch LED,LCD,OLED,Plasma Flat Screen,Curved TVs,Low Profile,Up to VESA 600x400 and 165 lbs,Fits 16",18",24" First let me get the positive out of the way. Very easy to assemble, sturdy, and I like the fact that I can secure the TV on the wall by the top as well as pop it free by unlocking the unit by pulling the two chains s on the bottom. It was very easy to assemble, and I like the fact that they gave you a leveler to make sure its straight. The images I posted is a 75-inch TV, the maximum it can hold is apparently an 80. However, the bigger you go, the harder it gets to reach behind the back to tilt it. There is still 2 1/2 space to run wires and reach around to turn the knob to tilt it forward or backwards.

Now the CON.

I was not planning on tilting this unit forward or backwards because it's a big tv. For those looking for a decent mount and plan on doing the exact same thing having it flat, with a little space behind it so that you can reach around and run the wires the two inches and a half for me of space was perfect. I secured the tilting mechanism to keep it facing forward. which are the two metal knobs as you see in my second uploaded image as well as Amazon's version in the photos. I figured that since it had two turning knobs it was the same as the previous one I owned that had a spinning knob that went forward unlock, and backwards lock. I installed some LED lights on the back of the TV and hung it on the mount 1 month later. However I decided to remove the LED lights on the unit without taking the whole TV off the wall because I can easily take those off by just pulling the lights off.

This is where the problem started and noticed the manufacturing or designer error, hopefully they can correct it in the future. When I pulled the LED off, it tilted the TV slightly upwards, no idea why when it was apparently secured facing forward when I tried reaching around to the side to turn the nob I noticed the little ball fell out of the turning metal nob. The ball that goes into the metal unit was super glued on and it's not a turning ball where you can put it in there, screw in to permanently secure it in place to metal rod.

This created a problem when I wanted to tilt the TV forward, I had to move the metal rod because now the ball fell off it and it could not be attached again because it was held in place by super glue when you turn the knob, the whole unit would slide through falling off. Also if you notice in the picture, it's three separate parts. Not only was the metal rod with the ball superglued on but the unit that you used to turn in place unscrews off because there's no resistance or warning mechanism when you're turning the knob you don't know which way to turn to tilt it.

Since I was trying to figure out which way to make it go forward and backwards I realized that the whole unit was unscrewing because I could keep turning it in a direction until the whole metal rod as well as the screw / nob came completely off. This means that I now had to reattach it back to the unit screw it back in as well as dealing with the ball that had fallen off the stick. I ended up just removing both of them and physically moving the TV by hand forward and upwards luckily it didn't require a lot of force and it must have been slightly loose.

Regardless of all that I would still recommend the unit. It is sturdy it's nice and I like the adequate space behind it or I can reach around the problem is that if you have a big TV and you plan on constantly tilting it forward and backwards before attaching it on the wall. it's probably better for you to tilt the TV and then attach it to the wall because reaching around the 75 inch TV it's a little bit more difficult easier to run a wire because you have more than enough space but harder if you want to reach the handle to tilt it forward and backwards.

Also in the setup video instructions, it's simply rotates the nob without saying counterclockwise lock, counterclockwise relock etc etc. There's also no resistance mechanism that would tell you it can't go forward. So what ends up happening is that you can unscrew the whole nob bar off by mistake leaving the screw on the mount and nob in your hand. Hopefully in a future revision. They use a ball screw to the nob vs super glue it and possibly secure the metal bar to the unit to where it can't be unscrewed off. But I think the best thing to do is it just properly aligned with television to your seating position and set it up like normal straight to avoid having to use the tilting mechanism.
text_fidelity_b: Everstone Adjustable Tilt TV Wall Mount Bracket for Most 32-90 Inch LED,LCD,OLED,Plasma Flat Screen,Curved TVs,Low Profile,Up to VESA 600x400 and 165 lbs,Fits 16",18",24"

text_fidelity_a:
Sony Cybershot DSC-S600 6MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom This is a point and shoot, so don't expect it to act like a DSLR or even an ultra zoom, but for what it is, it's a fantastic camera.

It starts up quickly and focuses very, very quickly. An AF assist lamp helps with this. The flash is strong and the image quality is very good. The LCD is smaller than most of the competitors in the upper range of the price bracket, but the screen is sharp and very clear. The AA batteries are great because they're cheap and easy to find. I hate it when I'm on a trip and want to shoot a lot, but have to be tethered to a wall socket to charge a battery. The movie mode is wonderful. TRUE 640x480 resolution at 30fps (only with the Pro Duo card) to the limit of the card. I like to take my movies, edit them with a program and burn them to DVD. 480 lines of resolution is TV quality and it looks GOOD. The only real downside to this camera is its bland styling. Other companies are making hot, slim, metal cameras that look good and are difficult to hold, but this camera's plastic body is sturdy and easy to carry in one hand. It has a pleasant weight to it, even if it's a little too wide to fit in a shirt pocket.

There are several websites dedicated to reviewing digital cameras in depth and they can give you technical numbers to compare with other cameras. Since I'm just a guy that occasionally takes photos, I can only talk about my experiences. I like the photos that this takes, I like the way it holds and functions and I like the clarity and smoothness of the movie mode...you really can't compare Sony camera movies to other companies' movie clips; Sony wins, hands down. Sony knows how to cater to their consumers and this camera won't disappoint!

I highly recommend it!
text_fidelity_b: Sony Cybershot DSC-S600 6MP Digital Camera with 3x Optical Zoom

text_fidelity_a:
Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation UPDATED March 11, 2015--See Below

SHOULD YOU BUY THIS UNIT?
In my opinion, this unit, like all things Amazon, is only about 80% ready for market but they release this stuff anyway. It's a cheap shot to their customers and they should straighten up and actually release products when they have all the features advertised actually implemented.

Buy this thing only if USB isn't important to you AND if you are willing to wait hours to upload video and picture content to the Amazon Cloud Drive. ABOUT THE CLOUD DRIVE--the initial allocation of space for your account is only a few gigs (I think 2 gigs). After that you can upgrade and pay Amazon more money for the bump up in storage space. That this unit has a non-functioning, flaccid USB forces you to use their cloud for video streaming your own stuff and this works for Amazon because lots of folks will end up paying for more cloud storage. This is borderline unethical in my opinion.

Pros:
Sets up easily.
Great help videos
Outstanding picture quality
WiFi and Wired connections both very good
Small footprint

Cons:
USB not implemented so you cannot play your own video content without uploading to their cloud
Uploading to their Cloud takes much longer than other clouds (Dropbox for example). It's hours compared to minutes
Puny cloud storage allocation without upgrade
Search has no QWERTY layout to type in your search and no way to add a space and second or more words to the search
Limited on-line support

CONCLUSION: Not really ready for prime time if you need full functionality in a unit like this.

UPDATED March 11, 2015: REDUCING THIS TO TWO STARS. Okay, this is the most annoying, frustrating and unreliable piece of technology I've ever purchased. In the months since I bought this item its performance has degraded to where it is simply unacceptable. Amazon tech support is of little help and neither is Netflix tech support. Here are the NEW FEATURES my Fire TV now performs:

1) Regularly pauses an in-progress program as if I'd pressed the pause button. It usually resumes after I press the play button on the remote.
2) It does not play nice with Netflix and often (actually daily) gets hung so that I see an error message telling me there's trouble, "playing this video right now...," and suggests I try later or pick something different. Well, I don't want to wait, nor do I wish to watch something else.
3) It often cannot find my HDMI cable, even though I've tried several cables. It is, therefore, not a cable problem but an internal glitch in the Fire TV box.
4) Often after turning it on, it goes to a blank screen from which there is no return.
5) There are many more fun things this piece of garbage does but why bother list them.

Tomorrow, I'm going to Best Buy to pick up a Roku 3 for about what it sells for on Amazon. See, then I won't have to wait for it to be shipped and, if necessary, I can take it back to a real store and exchange or return it. Oh, and I intend to donate this Fire TV box to the garbage can. I do hope it won't offend the garbage man/woman/person/whatever.
text_fidelity_b: Amazon Fire TV - 1st Generation

text_fidelity_a:
Jabra Elite Active 75t True Wireless Bluetooth, Navy – Earbuds for Running and Sport, Charging Case Included, 24 Hour Battery, Active Noise Cancelling Earbuds Pros--
-Very comfortable and secure fit even during high intensity exercise
-Solid Bluetooth connection
-Good noise canceling
-Hear thru mode is useful
-Sleek, low profile look
-Decent battery life, charging case is nice
-mic works well for calls or voice commands
-LOTS of bass (I consider this a major negative, but some people will like the bass heavy sound)

CONS-
-Below average sound quality (WAY too much bass, even after using the EQ to turn down the bass its still more than I would prefer for most types of music, the default out of the box sound is the worst I have ever heard on a pair of headphones in this price range.. but that said you can make them sound pretty decent after a bit of tweaking with the EQ)
-Not loud enough, the maximum volume is barely adequate for high external noise situations like airplane (even with the noise cancellation which works pretty well)
-Sealed design is not good for 'active' pursuits because of microphonic effect amplifying internal sounds whenever you move around
-software can be buggy, occasionally when I change settings and they appear to be changed in the software but do not apply to the buds

I think there are certain people who will love these buds, especially if you listen to a lot of rap/hiphop or other bass heavy music as the default sound seems to be tuned for that kind of music. Personally I just can't really get into the sound of these, even after tweaking with the EQ there is too much bass and the soundstage is flat and lifeless. I do like a lot of things about them though, the fit is comfortable and very secure, much better than airpods or galaxy buds on that front.

text_fidelity_a:
Bluetooth Speaker with LCD Display, NFC, FM Radio and Subwoofer Effect- Shower Speaker with Crystal Clear Sound and 3 Firm Suction Cups – Hands Free Speakerphone … (Red) [[VIDEOID:413906e1ac04fb2e066baa4adca5a20a]] This Bluetooth Shower Speaker with LCD Display by Abco Tech is the first shower speaker I've ever tried, so I can't compare it to any other one. I can share my impression of it from the perspective of one who hasn't used this sort of product before though and I hope that will be helpful to some of you who also haven't tried one before.

First of all, it measures 5 x 5 x 5 inches, and needs to be charged by USB after you receive it. Once it's charged you can attach it to a non-porous surface via three large suction cups in the rear of the speaker. We weren't able to get it to stick to our tile but it did attach firmly to the inside of the glass shower door and has held for three days so far without slipping or falling despite opening and closing the door.

The control buttons are easy to understand and operate. When you turn it on it makes a fairly loud beep, then the LCD display turns on and displays the time. I find having the clock very useful when trying to get kids out of the shower in time for school by the way! It has an integrated FM radio and you can preset up to 10 of your favorite stations and switch between them easily using the rewind and fast forward buttons. If you want to find different stations it will also do seek. When you select the radio mode it beeps loudly once again and then plays the station. Reception varies depending on signal strength, weather conditions and all the usual reasons. The default sound level is high but it's easy to adjust using the control buttons on the speaker.

Bluetooth: We had no problem pairing it to my daughter's iPhone 4S and streaming Pandora. In fact, the sound quality is excellent we thought! Once again the default sound level is high, but you can adjust that with the control buttons. ** It seemed as though we had problems getting it to switch to Bluetooth in the video, but that was because my daughter forgot to turn her phone back on for a moment. Once she did you can hear how good it sounded.** When you get a phone call while listening to the speaker it displays the calling phone number so you can decide whether to take the call or not, and if you decide to take it the speaker acts as a speakerphone.

Charge: So far it's been up for three days and we haven't had to charge it again, but then again we're only using it when in the shower or bathroom for longer periods of time so length of time it will hold the charge will vary depending on your usage. The rubber charging port cover doesn't want to stay covering the port up though, but it doesn't appear to have an effect on the speaker working.

We're very pleased by the quality, sound quality, and the features offered by this Bluetooth shower speaker so far. If anything changes I will update this review. I did receive a retail sample provided for evaluation and review consideration. I hope being able to see the actual speaker in position and working helps you to make a better informed buying decision. If you have any questions feel free to ask them in the comments section below and I'll try to respond as soon as I can. :)
text_fidelity_b: Bluetooth Speaker with LCD Display, NFC, FM Radio and Subwoofer Effect- Shower Speaker with Crystal Clear Sound and 3 Firm Suction Cups – Hands Free Speakerphone … (Red)

text_fidelity_a:
Seagate FreeAgent Go 320 GB USB 2.0 Portable External Hard Drive ST903203FAA2E1-RK (Black) I've been using an external Seagate drive for a few years for my daily backups, and it's worked great. However, it's not very portable (about the size of a thick paperback) and needs AC power. So, looked at what Seagate offers in a smaller size, and came across the FreeAgent Go.

It got good reviews in the computer mags and, after using it for a few days, I don't have a single complaint. It's tiny - very easy to toss into a laptop bag. It's powered from the USB port, so there's no need for a separate power connector or bulky transformer.

The included cable is pretty short -- bit over a foot long (didn't measure it - just a ballpark guess). I also bought the docking station which includes a much longer cable that has two connectors. I've not had any problems running the drive off my Dell Vostro with just a single connecter, but the double connector would come in hand should your PC not provide sufficient power over a single USB port. The docking station also comes with a carry case for the drive. Nothing fancy, but it's padded to help the drive survive being tossed about.

I have not installed any of the included software (looks like there's some backup and file synch software, plus encryption stuff). I'm using other software for that, so drive installation consisted of plugging it into a USB port, waiting a second for the PC to recognize it, then it's ready to go. About as easy as it gets!

The lights are kind of cool -- the case has a starburst-like pattern of lights that serves as the operation indicator. The lights fade in and out when the drive is operating. A bit more interesting than the usual single LED-type indicator.

Very pleased, and hope it will be as reliable as my other external Seagate. But, in case it's not, there's a five year warranty from Seagate.

Highly recommend!
text_fidelity_b: Seagate FreeAgent Go 320 GB USB 2.0 Portable External Hard Drive ST903203FAA2E1-RK (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Google Pixel Slate 12.3-Inch 2 in 1 Tablet Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 128GB, Aspect Ratio 3:2 The Pixel Slate is Google's computer of the near future. It is great for some people right now, but not for everyone. Google has had their Android tablets and Chromebooks for many years now. The Pixel Slate combines those two concepts into an evolving platform. The hardware is really great right now with great fit-and-finish, a very sharp colorful screen, very responsive touch sensors, and great sound quality. Battery life is very good (over 10 hours per charge). The software is evolving quickly. Google has already released many updates the Chrome operating system and I expect this to continue.

The main problem with the software is that the Pixel Slate is running two types of apps: Chrome browser web-apps and Android apps. The user interfaces for these two are slightly different, which can lead to user confusion. There are also interoperability problems between the two, which also leads to user confusion. For example, Android apps can share files by just clicking on the share icon. Sharing a file from a web-app to an Android app requires downloading the app to the local file system, then opening the Android app and hunting through the file system to find and open the file. Hopefully one day some kind of automatic sharing mechanism will be implemented. Another confusion is that some web-apps and Android apps have the same name and functionality, but don't work the same. For example, Amazon Kindle has both a web-app and an Android app. If I download a book in the Kindle Android app, the Kindle web-app cannot find it, so I have to remember to use the Kindle Android app.

Who should buy a Pixel Slate? Google initially announced 4 versions of this product: one with a Celeron CPU, one with a Core m3 CPU, one with a Core i5 CPU, and one with a Core i7 CPU. I have the i5 version, which is plenty fast and responsive for anything I'm trying to do (I am not a gamer).

Apparently, the performance of the Celeron version was so bad that product has been cancelled. Prices now range from $800 to $1600, not including accessories like the keyboard or stylus. Even the $800 version is a lot of money, especially when you consider that a very good Chromebook can be had for much less money and that has a built-in keyboard. I have to imagine that the only people who should consider the Pixel Slate instead of a high-end Chromebook are people who will regularly need to use this device as a lightweight tablet. At just a pound or so, the Pixel Slate's tablet mode is much lighter weight and much less bulky than any Chromebook, even those flip-over style Chromebooks. If you can't imagine life without a physical keyboard, then get yourself a good Chromebook instead of the Pixel Slate.

The physical keyboard is not included with the Pixel Slate. Amazon sells a couple of different versions, but both have flaws, as well as very high prices. For now, I'm using a Belkin USB keyboard when I'm using the Pixel Slate at my desk. When I'm on the go, I use the tablet in touch screen mode without a physical keyboard. If a better physical keyboard comes along, I'll rethink this setup.
text_fidelity_b: Google Pixel Slate 12.3-Inch 2 in 1 Tablet Intel Core i5, 8GB RAM, 128GB, Aspect Ratio 3:2

text_fidelity_a: Pioneer Electronics Audition Series XW_NAS3-K Docking Station for iPod (Black) I was the happy owner of the original Bose sounddock for seven years until it stopped working this November.  I thought that was a very good run.  To replace the Bose I chose the Pioneer NAS3 and waited a month for the price to drop to $220.  I like the clean design as I wasn't looking for a display nor was I looking for an alarm clock.  On first play I was not at all impressed with the muddy flat sound until I found that under the music menu on the ipod is a setting for 'speakers'.  Going into 'speakers' I can enhance the sound with the bass/treble on setting which is comparable to the ipod EQ acoustic setting.  You can really bump up the sound by turning on both but for me the sound becomes unnaturally bright and the bass distorts.  In other words the dock does respond to all ipod EQ settings.  Under 'speakers' I can also set the ipod display to always be on, always be off, or only come on when I press a key on the dock or on the remote.  Speaking of the remote, the range is strangely bad as you need to point it almost directly at the unit.  To make the NAS bluetooth capable then you'll need to buy the adaptor separately.  I don't know if it's only the Pioneer adaptor that will work but if that's the case, it's a pricey option at about $70. If this were an issue for me I would have rated the Pioneer three stars.  The sound quality here just doesn't earn it a five-star rating but I'll be keeping the unit.  If I had it to do it over again I would go with another Bose.
text_fidelity_b: Pioneer Electronics Audition Series XW_NAS3-K Docking Station for iPod (Black)

text_fidelity_a:
Nikon D5000 12.3 MP DX Digital SLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6G VR Lens and 2.7-inch Vari-angle LCD My D5000 was delivered yesterday evening while I was at work. The lovely wife opened the box enough to pull the battery out and charge it for me. After a grueling 12 hour shift at work I had forgotten about my new toy.

I had purchased the D5000 w/ 18/55 kit lens then separately purchased a 55/200 VR kit lens. It was cheaper that way. Go figure.

After many doggie slobbers when I arrived home I noticed the D5000 box on the kitchen table. My heart started palpating. I tried to control my self to no avail. My new toy was here! I carefully unpacked everything. I actually followed the quick start guide and was ready in no time.

I'm a big guy with the requisite big hands. The D5000 felt good in my hands. Not too heavy, not too light. The black body was finished with a slightly rough tactile coating. Very nice. My right thumb fit nicely in the thumb spot while my right index finger felt at home on the shutter. With a firm grip on the D5000 I was able to fully articulate my wrist and point the camera in a variety of positions. The camera felt good in my hand. I could tell that I could lug this beauty around for a full day and not get the dreaded "photog's wrist syndrome."

I attached the 18/55 kit lens. The lens seemed to provide a better balance when attached to the body. The VR switch, on the lens, was factory set to OFF. My first few images didn't utilize the VR. I was so excited and getting more excited by the minute that I forgot the properly look at the lens. I could notice the difference between the VR switching. This 18/55 kit lens is quite amazing. Sure it's made out of plastic, but it does a great job. If you don't already have Nikon lenses then the 18/55 kit lens is a no brainer. Well worth it.
As the quick guide said...Frame your first subject...then BAM!

I was looking for subjects to shoot. Since I work nights everyone, except the dog, was asleep. So I can't run around flipping light switches, move knick-knacks, or anything that could involve waking the baby. God forbid I wake the baby. My wife would have my testicles drawn and quartered within 7.9 seconds. Of course it's been raining for 2 days straight. So I'm stuck in the house...with a new camera. No worries!

I really like the D5000. Coming from the "superzoom point & shoot world" this is a welcome, although a little scary, change. I used film SLR cameras up until the late 90's so I have some experience with SLR photography. But the digital advances sure make everything so much easier. I'm not a "all manual all the time" kind of guy. Like most of us, I want the added feature of full-manual to play with, but like having an excellent and fast AUTO feature. I like to spend time with my family when we're all out and about and don't like to fiddle with any settings. The family gives me plenty of time, on my own, to experiment.

I added some images above.
text_fidelity_b: Nikon D5000 12.3 MP DX Digital SLR Camera with 18-55mm f/3.5-5.6G VR Lens and 2.7-inch Vari-angle LCD
