BAOFENG BF-F8HP (UV-5R 3rd Gen) 8-Watt Dual Band Two-Way Radio (136-174MHz VHF & 400-520MHz UHF) Includes Full Kit with Large Battery Received as a Christmas gift. As I am not a licensed ham yet I have not transmitted on the radio, so I can't speak about any transmission issues that others may have experienced. To date I have only used it to monitor ham radio bands to understand how hams communicate.

For an affordable introductory ham radio, Baofeng radios are a good choice. Some ham "purists" seem to have nothing good to say about them, but many hams are welcoming of new operators and understand that these radios have the potential to expand the hobby.

The radio comes with a decent book (when ordered from BAOFENG TECH). There are also quite a few resources and videos online to assist in usage.

I found programming of stations to be fairly simple although a bit time consuming. There isn't really that much to it. If you are going to program in multiple channels or set offsets for repeater use then a programming cable would be a good investment. The programming cable also allows you to name individual channels.

There are some potential issues that can occur with use of this radio.

1. This radio covers VHF and UHF ham bands but also conflicts with police bands, city maintenance, and private corporation radio frequencies. There is the potential to accidentally transmit on an unauthorized band.

2. While this radio will scan UHF/VHF police, fire and EMT bands most have shifted to a new system. Some agencies are on the older systems and some simulcast on UHF/VHF but in general if you are planning on using this as a police scanner you probably aren't going to hear much.

3. There is no way to lock out the transmit key, so it is easy to press it while handling the radio if not paying attention.

As a monitoring radio the battery seems to last forever. If you are planning on transmitting a lot then an extra battery or 12VDC adapter may be warranted.

So far I really don't have anything negative to say. Good introductory radio.
text_fidelity_b: BAOFENG BF-F8HP (UV-5R 3rd Gen) 8-Watt Dual Band Two-Way Radio (136-174MHz VHF & 400-520MHz UHF) Includes Full Kit with Large Battery

text_fidelity_a:
Garmin Forerunner 910XT GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate Monitor - Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer) As many have already written this watch has software issues. It does not display pace accurately. There's absolutely NO EXCUSE for Garmin releasing a training watch that doesn't know a person's pace. That's the sole reason this is getting a one star rating. On top of this, it is a simple software fix that they have still failed to make.

There is a simple work around: don't display pace and instead display lap pace. Lap pace has no issues and accurately describes your current pace. All the other pace features also work. Lap pace, ave pace, last lap pace are all accurate. The fact that everything else works fine shows to me it is just a software issue that Garmin could pretty easily fix if they bothered to spend 10 minutes on the issue. I probably would have given it four stars without this issue.

Why I really, really like this watch:

I bought this to supplement/replace my 405CX

The display is bigger and better. You can display four metrics at a time across four screens - so 16 metrics. The font is BOLD and easy to see even in tough conditions. While working out, you can hit the down or up arrow to more quickly get the screen you want to see. Also, even at its smallest, the font is bold and readable even to old eyes that don't see up close so well. The font describing each display is too small for my eyes to see when I have contacts in. So, I need to memorize which spot displays what. Still, this is sooo much better than the 405CX. On that watch, I can only see the big middle display with my contacts in.

The watch vibrates alerts. This is awesome!! I hate watches beeping at me and in loud conditions I would miss the beeps. I much prefer the vibration and I just turn off the audio alerts altogether. Also, the watch now alerts you (via beep or vibrate or both or none - your choice) when it has a GPS lock. The 405 never did this. Awesome improvement.

The battery lasts forever. Well probably not forever but you can use it for an entire day with GPS. The manual claims 22 hrs - I've yet to use it up when I started fully charged. The 405 claimed 8 hrs but it was really more like 6. Also, the 910 can be turned off so you can NOT waste the battery during travel time to your work out starting point.

It shows your recovery heart rate about one minute after you push 'stop' if you don't do the reset count downtime. Someone else mentioned that here. It a wonderful feature and not mentioned at all in the promotional material or users manual.

No touch bezel. The touch bezel in the 405 and 510 is a miserable feature. It has a life of its own in humid conditions which pretty much describes most of the heavily populated USA during most of the months of the year folks train a lot outside. The 910 completely relies on pushing buttons so now it only does things when you WANT the watch to do something. Also, the start/stop/lap/reset buttons are on the face of the watch. Everything else is on the sides. This keeps me from accidently hitting the wrong button when I don't mean to.

GPS programming seems smarter than the 405 / 510. With the 405 or 510 if you stop your movement and forget to hit stop on the watch it will keep adding distance. (For example, you can sit on a bench for a 15 minute break and it will add 0.5 miles to your distance.) I think this is because of GPS not knowing your exact location so it keeps seeing you as 10-20 feet from the last place it thought you were and keeps adding this up even though you are not moving. The 910 seems to do a lot less of this. It's still adds a bit of distance but over a 15 minute break it might be 0.05 miles instead of 0.5 miles.

Other things to note:

This watch is NOT smaller than other Garmin watches but it does stick out from your wrist less but to make up for that it is wider and taller. My guess is that it weighs pretty much the same. If you have a tiny wrist like mine, it can actually be a bit too big for your wrist. I got the cloth strap - this makes that issue much better.

I have not used it for swimming and I don't think I'm going to. It's not worth the risk if there is even a chance of screen fogging.

The manual not very useful. It doesn't show all the features. It is close to unintelligible. If I hadn't already had the 405 and was sorta familiar with how Garmin watches were organized, I'm not sure if I could have figured this out. Garmin's online help is no better.

Hint for female users: I skipped the heart rate monitor that came with the watch and instead got the original plastic hr monitor. I take off the strap and just place the main plastic part inside to top of my bra. It works great this way and is much more comfortable than having a strap wrapped around me and much easier to get in and out of and you don't have to find a private place to do it. I'm not sure if this will work for all women but it might be worth trying if you hate have a bra, HR monitor strap, plus shirt all binding around you like I do.

ETA 04-Jun-2012

I have found that lap pace isn't accurate either. Very disappointing. My latest work around is to reduce by lap distance to 0.25 miles. Last lap pace is accurate so by setting my laps as a very short distance, I'm getting constant feedback on my pace. Still, I think for a serious training regime, this wouldn't work. It's close enough for me.

(When I say not accurate, I mean not remotely accurate. It will show my pace as 10 minutes slower than I am going and it will stay that way for a full lap. Only when the lap is complete - it then shows total time for the lap correctly. It's not 5 minutes fast for half the time and 5 minutes slow for half the time. It's just off all the time and usually shows me as going at a pace 5-10 minutes slower than I am actually moving.)

On the a positive: another feature I'm really, really liking is the ability to manually scroll through the metric screens. I now set the screens to not scroll at all. I just use the up and down button and they get me to any screen I need. It's very nice for when all I care about is say, my heart rate. I just leave it on my HR screen but if I happen want to know my distance, then I can scroll to that screen and then back to my HR screen.

I'm also really, really still loving the giant display numbers. I can read these in any conditions. Rain, darkness, poor light, as I'm moving fast and don't have time to hold my hand still, etc.

ETA 09-Sep-2012
Garmin's support website has a post from 16-Aug-2012 that claims to have fixed the pace issue with a firmware update. I'm downloading it now. I'm planning an 11 mile hike today. I will post again if this fixes the issue.

See Garmin's site > tech support > search on 910 > search on 'pace issues.' Sorry, amazon removed the url.

BTW - I'm still using the 910 over the 405 despite the pace issue. The display and button functionality/placement of the 910 is just so superior to the 405 that it's worth the pace problems. I took my lap distance down to 0.10 miles so I get near continuous feedback on my pace that way.

Update 10-Sep-2012
The pace issue does seemed to be fixed!!! Or least, highly improved. The pace keeps nice and steady. It takes a few seconds of a changed pace for the watch to pick up on it which seems totally reasonable. Clearly there needs to be a lot of smoothing for the math equations seeing as GPS accuracy is only 15-20 feet and it only takes a reading every few seconds. Downloading the update is odd and I wasn't 100% sure it took but it does seem to have. My watch now displays my version as 2.6.

Upping my stars to five.

Update 07-July-2013.

With much trepidation, I just starting using this for open water swims. I've only done two so far in fresh water lakes. No fogging. Distances seem accurate enough. Maps show it has me within 30-40 meters of my real location. So far so good. I have not tried it in a pool.

I've also started using it on a bike. Just on my wrist. Lots of fun seeing how fast I'm going, etc but have yet to use it for any disciplined training. Just starting out but I really like it for this so far.

Also - Pace issue still seems fixed. It isn't as good as the old 405 but it also doesn't eat battery strength like the 405 did. I'll take the trade off.

Update 23-Dec-2014
I continue to heavily use this. Now the light has stopped working. It's past its warranty now. I'm reluctant to send it in to get fixed because I'm in training and don't want to be without it. It can be hard sometimes to get the charger attached these days. The attach points are extremely well worn at this point. I've used it 20+ time for swimming and have had no issues with fogging like some others have reported.
text_fidelity_b: Garmin Forerunner 910XT GPS Multisport Watch with Heart Rate Monitor - Black (Discontinued by Manufacturer)

text_fidelity_a: SamData 32GB USB Flash Drives 4 Pack 32GB Thumb Drives Memory Stick Jump Drive with LED Light for Storage and Backup (4 Colors: Black Blue Green Purple) This unit does work, but it is too slow for me to recommend it to others. When writing music onto it from my Windows computer, the write speed was slow enough to repeatedly drop the data transfer rate all the way to zero. Other manufacturers' flash drives do not do that; they keep on going. The read speed is slow enough that it causes my car's infotainment system (2019 model year) to sometimes hang up. Indeed, at one point, it caused my backup camera to go to all black for a minute or two. Note that some other reviewers are apparently unware of what flash memory is like. It has a limited number of times that it can be written (rewritten), and it will wear out if you try to use it as a substitute for a SSD. It also isn't going to be nearly as fast as a SSD. Flash memory is most appropriate for putting mp3 files into your car's infotainment system and other applications that are write only a few times but read many times.
text_fidelity_b: SamData 32GB USB Flash Drives 4 Pack 32GB Thumb Drives Memory Stick Jump Drive with LED Light for Storage and Backup (4 Colors: Black Blue Green Purple)

Tripp Lite 550VA UPS Battery Backup, 300W Eco Green, USB, RJ11, 8 Outlets (ECO550UPS), Black Like everyone in California, we've been having a lot of power outages and spotty power, and through that, I've been really made aware how important it is to have steady, continuous power to my devices and not be affected by brownouts or power surges. I also really appreciate that when the power goes out suddenly, I have enough time to save my work, print a document, or do any last critical wrap up before things go dark. This battery backup has been great!

If you have used battery backup in the past you generally know what to expect, you plug it into the wall, plug in your devices, and when the power goes out you have a little bit of time, depending on which devices are sapping power from it and how much juice they take, to finish up what you are doing and shut down properly.

What is interesting to me about this one is that it has something that automatically powers down accessory devices like your monitor or scanner when the master device is off. So I have the one plug for the master device, which is my computer, and one plug that is on battery backup that will power down and accessory device like my monitor when my computer is not on, and three plugs that will power down accessory devices and not have them on battery backup, good for things like my scanner. While I haven't hooked up a power reader to determine exactly my savings, I do know for sure that some of these accessory devices are indeed using power when they are not being used, so I really appreciate the thoughtfulness of this.

There are also some regular plugs, some of which are battery backup and some not. This is perfect because there are ample plugs for everything and I can really set things up just the way I need so that my printer is not drawing battery power during a power outage unless I actually want it to.

It's working as expected and seems to be designed with care. I definitely recommend this.
text_fidelity_b: Tripp Lite 550VA UPS Battery Backup, 300W Eco Green, USB, RJ11, 8 Outlets (ECO550UPS), Black

Thermal Grizzly Kryonaut The High Performance Thermal Paste for Cooling All Processors, Graphics Cards and Heat Sinks in Computers and Consoles (1 Gram) It confuses me that many people tomshardware, Gamer's Nexus, LTT, der8auer, etc, use this paste and get fantastic results, while I get worse than stock results.

I re-pasted my Overpowered 15+ laptop and as you can see in the pictures, before the re-paste I got about 80-83°C maximum temperatures. While after the re-paste I got 85-87° maximum temperatures. I have re applied the paste several times and gotten the same results.

I also used this paste on my desktop (didn't take screenshots) with a delidded 8700k and a H115i extreme and the results were:

Arctic Silver 5: 64-65° max
Kryonaut: 66-67° max.

The fact that I used this paste on both my laptop and desktop, and have also re applied the paste multiple times, leads me to believe that I am using the paste right (since AS5 performs better, *consistently*). And instead that the Kryonaut that I got is fake or a bad batch.

Mudder Portable USB Light Laptop Light for Keyboard Flexible Stick Dimmable Touch Switch LED White Light Lamp for Laptop Computer PC (Black) This is one of those simple but really useful gadgets to have. It's an LED light but, instead of a single bulb or two, it has a row of 10 bulbs arranged in a 6 inch span. The light output at it's brightest level is very bright - actually too bright in that you'll hurt your eyes if you look at the bulbs when they are at full brightness.

You turn the light on by tapping the end of the "bulb stick." Touch once to turn it on/off, press and hold while it is on to adjust the brightness. This is very thin - the bulb end is about the width of a pencil - so it's easy to fold up and stow in a tablet or laptop bag. Excellent build quality, especially considering the price.

It has a standard USB connector on the end for power. I've been powering it with a small powerbank and it draws very little power - leaving it on for several hours barely made a dent in the powerbank charge level.

I find this very helpful when using a tablet at night. I can bend the stalk so the light shines where I want it (the attached keyboard) but not on the screen. It's easy to stow when not in use - no wires or bits that get tangled up. Great value for the price.

text_fidelity_a:
GolfBuddy GB-WT3 Golf GPS/Rangefinder Watch Black To answer the first obvious question, yes, it can be worn comfortably on even fairly thin man's wrists. And it looks surprisingly good for something with these features. It does look like a quality object and - although a little bulky - I don't think it will bother anyone used to wearing men's wristwatches. I'm still trying to decide if the fact that it says "Golf Buddy" on it is silly, but I guess not for someone into golf and showing off their toys.

Unfortunately, you cannot get full layouts of courses with this watch, nor can you study any aspects of the course until you are there. But it does give you some very pertinent information while on the fairway or the green. But this is the tradeoff between this and a big golf GPS - you get a more convenient, less cumbersome, and less likely to annoy your friends because you're pulling it out to play with it when you should be putting device, but without the full color maps, weather and other junk you could replicate on your cell phone. And actually, I think it's a pretty nice compromise - you don't want to get so engrossed in electronics while you're out enjoying nature and weather and sport.

I also really like that it can do some basic watch and pedometer features like stopwatch, sunup/sundown, and show you how fast you are walking/biking/riding. On the flip side, since it already has the GPS, clock, and a bunch of programming script, it seems like it should house a lot more of those features; I almost expected to have many menus to explore and new features to discover for some time, but this was not the case.

It has a crazy charging "station". These days, I prefer anything just have a micro USB port so I don't have to think about extra cables or charging devices, but that would be difficult to incorporate and retain its water resistance, so it's probably the right solution, except since it has a USB-A end anyway, it should come with a 5V rectifier (most - but not everybody - has excess of these lying around).

This is a pretty nifty device for an enthusiast of both golf and gadgets, who doesn't want to bog down the game by looking at their GPS screen all day long.
text_fidelity_b: GolfBuddy GB-WT3 Golf GPS/Rangefinder Watch Black

ZUGU CASE - 2019 iPad Air 10.5/2017 iPad Pro 10.5 inch Case Prodigy X - Very Protective But Thin + Convenient Magnetic Stand + Sleep/Wake Cover (Purple) Update: A good pencil sleeve to use with this case after stretching it out a bit with a crayola dry erase marker is the Hydream Silicone Case for Apple Pencil Holder Sleeve Skin Pocket Cover Accessories for iPad Pro 9.7/10.5/12.9, Cute Soft Grip Pouch with Charging Cap Holder and 2 Protective Nib Covers.

TL:DR - a fantastic case and looks amazing with a screen protector on the device. Does not interfere with screen protectors at all. Great utility and angle options. Looks good on the fridge too. If you don't mind the case feeling a bit awkward to hold when looking at things in portrait and the fact that your Pencil Sleeve options are limited due to the super tight elastic (I used a crayola dry eraser to stretch mine and now the fit perfect) this is the case for you.

Pros:
8 Adjustment points
The packaging and info included on the company
The quality
The looks (at least in black for me)
The pencil sleeve built in
The wake/sleep utility
Solid positions minus the last one if you're really pretty on it. Like heavy handed drawing hard.

Cons:
The tablet is hard to hold in portrait especially if the pencil is in the case
I know the 2018 Pro model had yet to be released when this case was made, but I wish the placement of the Pencil sleeve was in a better location or allowed enough space for a wider variety of pencil sleeves. It makes me worry that it sticks out a little from the case. Kinda wish it was on the top or had a similar elastic sleeve loop on the top where an Apple Pencil 2 would sit magnetically. More or a nitpick though.
The tightness of the sleeve out of the box! This was very annoying, but another nitpick since I can always stretch it out.
A little awkward to use the rear-facing camera since when holding with the front panel touching the back of the case it covers the camera completely. Even when in landscape you have to tilt it high enough to free your view.

Quality of Life Cons: (basically super nitpicks. Feel free to ignore. The case is great!)

Epson Home Cinema 5050UB 4K PRO-UHD 3-Chip Projector with HDR,White The 5050ube is an excellent upgrade on the Epson 5040 projector. It provides a significant upgrade on the pseudo-4k projector with an impressive 2600 lumens making it one of the brightest projectors out there easily surpassing the 1500 lumens you would get with the entry level Sony true 4K projector. One of the big upgrades is the move to 18Gbps bandwidth giving you the ability to do 4K at 60Hz. Note that you do need to have a wired connection to get the full 18Gbps -- you only get 12 if you do the wireless option that the 5050ube offers over the regular 5050ub. Even with the reduced bandwidth that you get with the wireless setup, it is a great convenience to have the ability to stream from sources without having to run a wire from the source to the actual projector.

Another great aspect of the 5050 is the motorized lens which is a feature that other more expensive true-4k projectors do not offer. Of course with Epson you do get exceptional HDR quality as well as amazing black.

This is an impressive pseudo-4K projector that provides features that are not even found in some entry level true 4K projectors. If you are not absolutely dying to get true 4k, then this should be one of the projectors you should consider.

text_fidelity_a:
Echo Show - 1st Generation Black I was really surprised by the Show. My first impression was that it's a little bigger than I expected. It's also fairly heavy. Now having used it a few months, I'm glad for the weight. As you are pecking the touch screen with your finger, the extra weight keeps it very stable.

I was anxious to get it started up and see how it's sound compared to my original Echo. I was surprised. I think it sounds better. It has a deeper bass response and the sound is a little more directional with the speakers being in the front.

Other features I really enjoy is that you can load a custom home image, and it constantly scrolls "trending" topics across the home page when not in use. If you see something you want to know more about, you can ask it and it will play the audio or video clip. If you miss something, you can ask it what's trending and it will list everything.

I love that most things you ask it will give the normal Alexa audio response, but also a visual. The weather is a good example. It reads the weather just as an Echo would do, but also shows you the visual on the screen and allows you to scroll through the days ahead with a touch of the finger.

I use it for video calling with a friend who also owns one and it works well. The audio quality is good and we're able to communicate face to face.

I search for and watch youtube videos quite often. If there is something specific you are looking for, it can be painful. The search doesn't always understand slang or complex words, making the search results a little unreliable.

Overall, I really like it. It doesn't "hear" better than the original Echo and does frequently respond when you aren't talking to it, just like the original. It just has a little better sound and a nice touch display screen!
text_fidelity_b: Echo Show - 1st Generation Black
